readerTitle: Why a refunded order costs more than a lost sale
caseNote: 가상 사례 (온라인 신발 가게, 가정 수리 서비스) · 모든 수치는 설명용 · 사이즈를 여러 개 주문하고 일부를 반품하는 행동은 일반적인 관찰로만 언급
insight: 반품은 취소된 판매가 아니라 돈이 드는 거래다. 반품을 줄이는 것이 주문을 늘리는 것보다 이익에 더 크게 작용할 수 있다.
misconception: 환불하면 판매가 없던 일이 되므로 반품의 비용은 0이거나 반송비 정도다.

sources.text: 운영·관리회계의 일반 개념 (반품 처리 비용, 역물류, 재작업·재방문 비용)

factChecks.note: 판매 1건이 남기는 돈: $80 − 제품 원가 $30 − 발송비 $8 − 포장 $2 = $40. 반품 1건 비용: 발송비 $8 + 포장 $2 + 반송 라벨 $8 + 검수·재포장 $4 + 재판매 손실 평균 $6 = $28. 재판매 손실 $6 = 반품 5켤레 중 1켤레가 $30 싸게 팔린다는 가정. 제품 원가 $30은 재고로 돌아오므로 비용에서 제외. 28 ÷ 40 = 70%.
가정 수리 서비스: 작업 10건 × $80 = $800, 재방문 1회 비용 $90 → $710. 재방문 1회가 작업 1건 이상의 이익을 없앤다는 문장 확인.
온라인 의류·신발 쇼핑에서 여러 사이즈를 주문하고 일부를 반품하는 행동은 널리 보고된 현상이지만, 카드에는 구체적 비율을 쓰지 않았습니다. 수치를 추가하려면 1차 출처를 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why a refunded order costs more than a lost sale
body: A customer orders shoes from your online shop, tries them on, and sends them back. You refund the full price.
It feels like the sale simply never happened. On your books, it's worse than that. You paid to ship, pack, receive and check a pair that earned you nothing.

image.label: A shoebox travelling to a door and back again
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 신발 상자 하나가 창고에서 집 문 앞까지 갔다가 다시 창고로 돌아오는 원형 경로. 경로 위에 작은 동전들이 떨어져 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고나 택배사 표시는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Grow orders, or cut returns?
body: Your shop sells shoes at $80. Each pair a customer keeps leaves you $40 after the product, shipping and packing. Right now 1 in 5 orders comes back.
You can fund one project this quarter. Which adds more profit?

options.feedback: More orders do add profit, but 1 in 5 of the new ones still comes back and costs you. The gain is smaller than it looks.

options.text: Better size guides that cut returns from 20% to 15%
options.feedback: Each avoided return saves a cost and keeps a $40 sale. That double effect makes this the bigger lever here, about 2.6 times bigger.

options.text: About the same, so pick the cheaper project
options.feedback: Reasonable if a return just cancels a sale. It doesn't. A return costs money on top of the sale you lose.

cards.title: Follow one returned pair.
body: The shoes come back to stock, so you don't lose the $30 product. But one return still costs about **$28**. That wipes out 70% of what a kept pair earns.

breakdown.label: Check and repack
breakdown.detail: Staff time to inspect each pair

breakdown.label: Resale loss
breakdown.detail: 1 in 5 returns is worn and sells $30 cheaper

breakdown.label: Cost of one return
breakdown.detail: Paid for a sale that earned nothing

cards.title: Profit per 100 orders
body: With no returns, 100 orders would leave $4,000. With 1 in 5 coming back, they leave $2,640.
Growing orders 5% adds $132. Cutting returns to 15% adds **$340**.

cards.title: The true cost of a return
body: A **return** takes back the revenue from a sale but not the costs. Shipping, packing and handling are already spent, and getting the item back adds new costs.
So a return isn't a zero. It's a negative. Each one costs you twice: the profit the sale would have left, plus the cost of undoing it.
That's why the return rate belongs next to price and cost when you judge what an order really earns.

image.label: A kept sale adds coins; a return removes them
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Kept: +$40" 저울에 동전이 쌓임. 오른쪽 "Returned: −$28" 저울에서 동전이 빠져나감. 가운데 "Not zero" 라벨. 단순한 평면 스타일.

cards.title: Most returns start before the sale.
body: Returns rarely come from bad luck. They come from a gap between what customers expected and what arrived: unclear sizing, photos that flatter, damage in transit.
Some customers order two sizes on purpose and send one back. They're not cheating. They're filling a gap your product page left open.
Closing that gap usually costs less than processing the returns it causes.
cards.softwareNote: The same math shows up as refunds and first-month cancellations. Each one can cost you the sales effort, onboarding time and payment fees, often with nothing back. Clear trial terms and setup help can be the cheapest fix.

cards.title: Zero returns is the wrong goal.
body: Easy returns reassure customers, and many buy only because they can send things back. A strict policy can cut returns and sales at the same time.
The goal is fewer *avoidable* returns: the ones caused by poor information, poor packing or poor fit. Fix those first.
And count returns honestly. If your reports show only the refund, every return looks free and every fix looks like a waste of money.

cards.title: Now it's a home repair business.
body: Your team fixes leaks and fits appliances. A typical job leaves $80 after labor and parts. About 1 in 10 jobs needs a callback: a second visit, unpaid, costing about $90 in time and travel.
That one callback wipes out more than a whole job's profit. What do you do?

options.text: Charge customers for callbacks from now on
options.feedback: You recover some cost, but customers see it as paying twice for one job. You may lose reviews and repeat work worth far more.

options.text: Add a short test and walk-through with the customer before leaving
options.feedback: It adds a few minutes to every job but catches problems while the technician is still there. Like a size guide, it closes the gap before it becomes a return.

options.text: Accept callbacks as normal and raise prices a little
options.feedback: It covers the cost on paper, but you keep paying for avoidable second visits and risk losing price-sensitive customers.

cards.title: A return is not a cancelled sale. It's a sale that cost you money.
body: Count what each return really costs, and fixing the cause often beats chasing more orders.
**Try it today:** take one recent return, refund or redo. Add up every cost it caused, not just the money you gave back.
